A greedy algorithm builds the solution one step at a time, **always taking what looks best right now**, and never looks back. It's fast — usually O(n log n) for a sort, then O(n) — but only *correct* when local choices provably don't ruin the future. ## The burden of proof Greedy = easy to code, easy to get wrong. Before trusting one, produce an argument. The workhorse is the **exchange argument**: > *"Suppose some optimal solution disagrees with my first greedy choice. Swap its choice for mine — nothing gets worse. Therefore some optimal solution agrees with greed. Repeat for every step."*
If you can't sketch that argument (or find a counterexample!), the problem probably isn't greedy — it's DP. ## Greedy vs DP | | Greedy | DP | |---|---|---| | Choices considered | one, irrevocable | all states | | Proof needed | exchange argument | overlapping subproblems | | Speed | usually O(n log n) | O(n·states) | | Typical failure | coins {1,3,4}, target 6 → greedy takes 4+1+1=3 coins; true answer is 3+3=**2** | handles it | That coin counterexample is worth memorizing — interviewers love asking "when does your greedy break?" ## The classic greedy shapes - Sort by some key, sweep once (intervals, capacity loading) - Track running best/worst while scanning (jump game reach) - Take from sorted ends / heaps repeatedly (rearrangements)
